read.sections.0.text.note: Politically sensitive: Indonesia's two dates (17 August 1945 proclamation, 27 December 1949 transfer of sovereignty). Translated closely and neutrally; please check that nothing suggests independence only began in 1949. Second pass: Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta are now written ซูการ์โน and โมฮัมหมัด ฮัตตา in Thai script, like the course's other well-known historical figures (การ์ตีนี, โกน), with the Latin once in the evidence cards (Source 1 caption and the 1945 timeline entry).
read.sections.0.text.source: On 17 August 1945, two leaders, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta, made a proclamation of independence for Indonesia. The country's National Archives keeps Sukarno's handwritten draft of this short text. For Indonesians, 17 August 1945 is the day of independence. But the Netherlands had ruled the islands as a colony, and it did not accept the proclamation. Years of armed struggle and talks followed. On 27 December 1949, the Netherlands transferred sovereignty. This was a different event from the proclamation. It came after a long struggle. The draft records the 1945 statement. It does not tell us about every talk, or how people lived through those years.
read.sections.0.text.back: On 17 August 1945, two leaders, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta, issued the proclamation of Indonesia's independence. The country's national archives keep this short draft text handwritten by Sukarno. For Indonesians, 17 August 1945 is independence day. But the Netherlands had ruled these islands as a colony and did not accept this proclamation. After that there were years of armed struggle and negotiation. On 27 December 1949, the Netherlands transferred sovereignty. This is a different event from the proclamation, and it came after a long struggle. The draft records the proclamation in 1945, but does not tell us about every negotiation, or how people lived through those years.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: On 17 August 1945, two leaders made a proclamation. They said Indonesia was free. The two men were Sukarno and Hatta. Sukarno wrote the first draft by hand. The national archives keep it today. The Dutch had ruled the islands as a colony. They did not accept the proclamation. Years of fighting and talks came next. In December 1949, the Dutch passed sovereignty to the new state. That was a new step, not the first one. But for the people there, 1945 is still the year they became free.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: On 17 August 1945, two leaders, Sukarno and Hatta, issued a proclamation. They said Indonesia was free. The first draft was in Sukarno's own handwriting. Today the national archives still keep this draft. The Dutch had ruled these islands as a colony. They did not accept the proclamation. Then there were years of fighting and negotiation. In December 1949, the Dutch transferred sovereignty to the new state. That was a new step, not the first step. But for the people there, 1945 is still the year they became free.

read.sections.1.text.note: Federation of Malaya: written สหพันธรัฐมาลายา, the course's spelling of Malaya (มาลายา, as in course.json and SAT05); the first draft's note said มลายา. The glossary word is สหพันธ์ from KEY_TERMS, which is not a substring of สหพันธรัฐ, so สหพันธรัฐ is a form and สหพันธ์ appears in “มาเลเซียซึ่งเป็นสหพันธ์ที่ใหญ่กว่า”. Malayan Emergency: ภาวะฉุกเฉินในมาลายา (check the usual Thai term).
read.sections.1.text.source: The Federation of Malaya took a different path. On 8 February 1956, its leaders and Britain signed an agreement in London. It set 31 August 1957 as the day of independence. These are not two rival dates. One is the date of an agreement, and one is the date it planned for. The new country was the Federation of Malaya. Malaysia, a larger federation, was formed later, on 16 September 1963. A path built on talks still had conflict. A long armed conflict called the Malayan Emergency began in 1948. It was declared over only in 1960.
read.sections.1.text.back: The Federation of Malaya took a different path. On 8 February 1956, leaders of Malaya and Britain signed an agreement in London. This agreement set 31 August 1957 as independence day. These two dates do not compete: one is the day the agreement was made and the other is the day the agreement planned. The new country at that time was the Federation of Malaya. Malaysia, a larger federation, was formed later, on 16 September 1963. A path built through negotiation still had conflict. A long armed conflict called the Malayan Emergency began in 1948 and was only declared over in 1960.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Malaya took a different path. In 1956, its leaders and Britain signed an agreement in London. It set a date. On 31 August 1957, the Federation of Malaya became free. A federation is a group of states that work as one. Malaysia came later, in 1963. Malaya's path used talks. But there was also a long armed conflict. It began in 1948. It did not end until 1960.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Malaya took a different path. In 1956, leaders of Malaya and Britain signed an agreement in London. This agreement set a date. On 31 August 1957, the Federation of Malaya became free. A federation is a group of states that work together as one. Later, in 1963, Malaysia was formed. Malaya's path used negotiation, but there was also a long armed conflict. This conflict began in 1948 and did not end until 1960.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Compare evidence, not countries as winners
read.sections.2.heading.back: Compare the evidence, not decide which country won

read.sections.2.text.source: The two paths had different people, papers, conflicts and choices. A proclamation, an agreement and a ceremony each record a different part of change. The photo shows Stadium Merdeka in Kuala Lumpur in 2025. It shows the place, not the 1957 ceremony. A British news film made on the day shows crowds, guests and the Federation's flag going up. When you compare sources, ask three questions. What happened on this date? Who made the source? What came later? A careful look can show how two paths differ, without calling one of them better.
read.sections.2.text.back: These two paths had different people, documents, conflicts and choices. A proclamation, an agreement and a ceremony each record different parts of the change. The photo shows Merdeka Stadium in Kuala Lumpur in 2025. It shows the place, not the ceremony in 1957. The British newsreel filmed on that day shows crowds, guests and the Federation's flag being raised. When you compare sources, ask three questions. What happened on this date? Who made this source? What happened after that? Looking carefully helps you see how the two paths are different without having to say which path is better.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: The two paths had different people and choices. A proclamation, an agreement and a ceremony each show one part of the story. The photo shows a stadium in 2025. It does not show the 1957 ceremony. A British film from 1957 shows crowds and a new flag going up. Ask three questions about each source. What happened on this date? Who made it? What came after? Do not say one path was better.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: These two paths had different people and choices. A proclamation, an agreement and a ceremony each show a different part of the story. The photo from 2025 shows the stadium. The ceremony in 1957 is not in this photo. The British film from 1957 shows crowds and the new flag being raised. Ask three questions of every source. What happened on this date? Who made it? What happened after that? Don't say which path is better.

write.example.source: For Indonesia, one dated record is the proclamation of 17 August 1945. The national archives keep Sukarno's draft of it. For Malaya, one dated record is the agreement signed in London in 1956. It set 31 August 1957 as the day Malaya became free. A proclamation is a public statement by the country's own leaders. A transfer of sovereignty is a later step. It is when the old ruler hands over power. Neither source tells us how every person lived in these years.
write.example.back: For Indonesia, one dated record is the proclamation of 17 August 1945. The national archives keep the draft Sukarno wrote. For Malaya, one dated record is the agreement signed in London in 1956. This agreement set 31 August 1957 as the day Malaya became free. A proclamation is a message that the country's own leaders tell everyone. A transfer of sovereignty is a step that happens later, when the former ruler hands over power. No source tells us how everyone lived during these years.

watch.summary.source: This short film was made in 1957 in Kuala Lumpur by British Pathé, a British company that made news films. It shows the ceremony for the independence of the Federation of Malaya. First, the camera looks down on Stadium Merdeka. The stadium is full of people, and many of them hold umbrellas. Cars arrive, and important guests walk in. The camera moves between the guests and the crowds. People make speeches from a raised stage. Guards stand very still around the field. Near the end, the flag of the Federation is raised. The important guests salute it as it reaches the top of the pole. The film shows one day. It does not show the years of talks that came before it.
watch.summary.back: This short film was made in 1957 in Kuala Lumpur by British Pathé, a British company that made newsreels. The film shows the independence ceremony of the Federation of Malaya. First, the camera looks down on Merdeka Stadium. The stadium is full of people, and many hold umbrellas. Cars arrive, and important guests walk in. The camera moves between the guests and the crowd. Someone gives a speech from a raised stage. Guards stand very still around the field. Near the end, the Federation's flag is raised. The important guests salute the flag when it reaches the top of the pole. This film shows one day, not the years of negotiation that happened before.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Both paths involved armed conflict: Indonesia's struggle of 1945–1949 and the Malayan Emergency of 1948–1960. The lesson names this plainly and gives no detail; keep it that way, and show no images of fighting. Many popular YouTube videos on Indonesia's revolution show combat and dead bodies, so do not swap one in for the Watch video. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, conflict or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and never ask them to compare their own country's history with these. Learners and staff in Indonesia or Malaysia may feel strongly about these dates: present each as that country's own history, not a contest.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Both paths had armed conflict: Indonesia's struggle in 1945–1949 and the Malayan Emergency in 1948–1960. The lesson says so directly without detail; keep it that way, and don't show images of fighting. Many popular YouTube videos about the Indonesian revolution show fighting and bodies, so don't use such videos in place of the Watch video. Do not ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, conflict or displacement, or about home country, religion or ethnicity, and don't have learners compare their own country's history with these. Learners and staff in Indonesia or Malaysia may have strong feelings about these dates. Present each story as that country's own history, not a competition.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners compare dated records for the two paths without ranking them. Evidence move: separate 1945 and 1949 for Indonesia, and 1956 and 1957 for the Federation of Malaya, then name 1963 for Malaysia. A sound answer gives a dated comparison and never says that one nation's independence depended only on outside recognition. Misconceptions to address: "Indonesia was only independent in 1949", "Malaya's path had no conflict", and calling 1957 "Malaysia's independence".

educatorNotes.1.note: Sensitive history for adults: the Dutch date versus the Indonesian date, the 2023 Dutch statement, the United States of Indonesia (สาธารณรัฐสหรัฐอินโดนีเซีย) and Malaysia's founding members. Please check it stays neutral and the state names are the usual Thai ones.
educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: Indonesians count independence from 17 August 1945. For decades the Netherlands named 27 December 1949 instead; the Dutch National Archives' teaching page notes that in 2023 the Dutch prime minister said the Netherlands fully accepts that Indonesia became independent on 17 August 1945. The 1949 transfer was to the federal Republic of the United States of Indonesia, replaced by the unitary Republic a year later: keep this in your notes, not as another date for learners. Malaysia was formed in 1963 by the Federation of Malaya, Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak (Brunei did not join). Government and archive pages on both sides use celebratory language; treat it as their perspective. FINAS's long film "Merdeka for Malaya" (1958) is a state-produced source to analyse, not a Watch video, and do not reproduce the National Archives of Malaysia's 1957 photograph without its reuse permission.
